findings.claim: All 48 practice questions, in all eight lessons, are typed “40 marks — Shakespeare Essay”.
findings.truth: Great Expectations is the 19th-century prose text on the modern and literary heritage paper. Shakespeare sits in the other component. Relabelled “40 marks — 19th-century prose essay”.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md section 3a: the 19th-century prose section is worth 40 marks; Shakespeare is in the poetry and Shakespeare component.

findings.claim: All 48 mark ladders are malformed: 46 read “Band 6: … / Lower bands: less detailed”, and two open “Top band (34–40)” with a stray “Upper band (26–33)” and “Bands 1–4”.
findings.truth: Neither ladder scales to the real 40-mark total and neither uses house band names. Rescaled to five equal house bands: Top (33-40), Upper-mid (25-32), Mid (17-24), Lower-mid (9-16), Low (1-8), keeping each question's own top-band content.
findings.evidence: House ladder rule; same rescale applied in the sibling OCR unit english-literature-ocr__war-of-the-worlds.

findings.claim: “Compeyson — who dressed like a gentleman — received fourteen years while Magwitch received life.” Repeated as flashcard 6: “Why does Compeyson receive 14 years while Magwitch gets life for the same crime?”
findings.truth: At that trial Compeyson got seven years and Magwitch fourteen. Magwitch was only sent for life after he escaped from the hulks and was re-sentenced.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 42: “when we’re sentenced, ain’t it him as gets seven year, and me fourteen”. Ch. 39: “I was sent for life. It’s death to come back.”

findings.claim: Magwitch quoted as “his white pocket handkerchief, and what a common sort of wretch I looked”.
findings.truth: The novel gives Magwitch dialect forms: “his white pocket-handkercher” and “a common sort of a wretch”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 42, lines 14724-14726.

findings.claim: “For OCR Component 01, always connect Victorian context…”
findings.truth: Component codes are banned in lesson fields. Replaced with “For the 19th-century novel question”.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md banned-string list.

findings.claim: “Pip steals food and a file from his sister’s kitchen and brings them to Magwitch.”
findings.truth: The food comes from the pantry; the file comes from Joe’s forge. The detail matters because the stolen file is Joe’s and it is the leg-iron file later used on Mrs Joe.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 2: “In the pantry… I stole some bread”; “got a file from among Joe’s tools”.

findings.claim: “He tells Pip: ‘we’d be good pals, wouldn’t us, Pip? If it warn’t for your sister.’” Repeated as flashcard 9.
findings.truth: Fabricated. Joe never says this; the word ‘pals’ is never in his mouth anywhere in the novel. His real line of solidarity is “Ever the best of friends; ain’t us, Pip?”
findings.evidence: Gutenberg: no match for ‘pals’ spoken by Joe; ch. 7 line 1999-2000 gives the real line.

findings.claim: “I took the opportunity of being alone in the courtyard, to look at my coarse hands and my common boots. They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me now.” Also printed as the extract on practice question 3.
findings.truth: The novel has no comma after ‘courtyard’, and the sentence “My opinion of those accessories was not favourable” sits between the two quoted ones, so the join needs an ellipsis.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 8, lines 2610-2613.

findings.claim: “Only to Joe does he confess the truth: ‘I wished Joe had been rather more genteelly brought up…’” Practice question 5 prints the same line as “Chapter 9, where Pip lies about Satis House”, and flashcard 15 calls it a “wish to Biddy”.
findings.truth: The line is Pip’s private narration in the Satis House courtyard in ch. 8. It is not the confession he makes to Joe in ch. 9, and it is not said to Biddy.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 8, line 2615.

findings.claim: “…his life there a source of ‘mortification.’ He tells us: ‘I used to want — quite painfully — to be a gentleman.’”
findings.truth: Both quotations are wrong. ‘Mortification’ is never Pip’s word for the forge, and ‘quite painfully’ belongs to a ch. 13 sentence about wanting to burst into tears and pummel Pumblechook. Pip’s real line is to Biddy in ch. 17: “I want to be a gentleman.”
findings.evidence: Gutenberg line 4084 (ch. 13) and lines 5352-5353 (ch. 17).

findings.claim: Practice question 4: “Read from Chapter 39, Magwitch’s speech: ‘I’ve come to the old country fur to see my gentleman spend his money like a gentleman.’”
findings.truth: The line is in ch. 40, the morning after the ch. 39 revelation.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 13928-13929; ch. 40 starts at line 13697.

findings.claim: “He is arrested and imprisoned.” Repeated in flashcard 7 as “debt-prison illness”.
findings.truth: Two officers do arrest Pip for debt, but he is too ill to be moved and they leave him where he is. He is never imprisoned; Joe pays the debt.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 57: “they forbore to remove me”.

findings.claim: “Her dress catches fire and she burns — a fitting symbolic death…” Repeated in flashcard 13: “Her bridal dress catches fire and consumes her.”
findings.truth: Pip throws his coats over her and smothers the flames. The surgeon judges her hurts “far from hopeless”; she is laid on the great table and speaks again. Joe reports her death much later.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 49, lines 16924-16960; ch. 57, lines 19551-19566 (“she ain’t living”, about a week after Pip fell ill).

findings.claim: “He becomes a snob, treating Joe with ‘a touch of reproach’…”
findings.truth: ‘A touch of reproach’ is what Pip feels towards Magwitch on the night of the revelation. It is not his manner towards Joe.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 39, line 13372.

findings.claim: Knowledge check 1: “Which assessment objectives does OCR Component 01 Section B test?”, with “AO1, AO2, and AO3” marked correct and “AO1, AO2, AO3, and AO4” marked wrong.
findings.truth: AO4 is assessed in the 19th-century prose section, so the option the check marked wrong is the right one. The stem also carried a banned spec code.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md section 3h: accurate spelling and punctuation (AO4) are assessed in Section B of each examined component.

findings.claim: Knowledge check 2: “How many marks is the Section B question worth?”
findings.truth: The answer (40) is right; only the section code needed replacing with house phrasing.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md banned-string list; spec section 3a gives 40 marks.

findings.claim: “Both require AO1 (response with textual references), AO2 (analysis of language/form/structure), and AO3 (context).”
findings.truth: AO4 is assessed on this question too. Teaching three objectives hides marks the student can win for accurate writing. The same paragraph also said the question ‘may offer’ a choice of two; the choice is fixed.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md sections 3a and 3h.

findings.claim: Exam tip: “OCR marks AO1, AO2, and AO3 together in a holistic band.” The glossary term ‘holistic marking’ repeats the same three-objective list.
findings.truth: Accurate writing is judged here as well. Rewritten without any per-objective mark numbers, because the spec publishes no marking grid and any split would be invented.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md section 3h.

findings.claim: Of the original ending: “She has remarried after Drummle’s death, and they part as strangers.” Repeated in knowledge check 5.
findings.truth: In the original ending Pip and Estella recognise each other and part with understanding, not as strangers; Pip says he saw that suffering had given her a heart. The remarriage and the brief London meeting are right. Left unedited: the original ending is not in the Gutenberg file and I had no primary source to quote.
findings.evidence: Not verifiable from scripts/_retrofc/_texts/great-expectations.txt, which prints only the revised ending.

findings.claim: Punctuation-only quotation variants: “He calls the knaves, Jacks, this boy!” (lessons 1 and 2), “impression of the identity of things, seems to me” (lesson 2 extract), “Break their hearts, my pride and hope” (lesson 2 and its flashcard), “She lived and found powerful friends” (lesson 5).
findings.truth: Gutenberg #1400 reads “knaves Jacks”, “of things seems”, “Break their hearts my pride and hope” and “She lived, and found powerful friends”. Commas only; printed school editions vary. Recorded, not edited, as in the sibling AQA Great Expectations unit.

findings.claim: Flashcard 1 asks “In which region are the marshes of Great Expectations set?” and answers “The Kent marshes”; flashcard 2 answers “The Kent marshes at dusk.”
findings.truth: The first question restates its own answer, and the two answers are near-duplicates. Not wrong, so recorded rather than rewritten.
findings.evidence: raw/L07.txt flashcards 1-2.

summary: Eight lessons checked against the Gutenberg text and the OCR J352 spec. Two unit-wide labelling faults: every one of the 48 practice questions was typed a Shakespeare essay, and every mark ladder was malformed (46 ‘Band 6 / Lower bands’, two mis-scaled 34-40 ladders). No per-AO mark split appears anywhere in the unit, and no lesson claims 30 marks, 45 minutes, a two-part question or a compulsory extract, so the marks, timing and question-choice facts were already right. The real content faults are three fabricated or misapplied quotations in lesson 2, Miss Havisham burned to death in lesson 6 when Pip saves her, Compeyson and Magwitch given the wrong sentences in lesson 1, and lesson 8 teaching that only three objectives are assessed — with a knowledge check that marked the true four-objective answer wrong. 122 edits written; three LOW items left as notes.
